chapters.title: Chapter 2: Government-Backed and Fixed Return Options

lessons.title: NSC and 5-Year Tax Saver Fixed Deposits

children.text: NSC and tax saver FDs are what your parents bought every March. They are simple, predictable and guaranteed. They also hide a catch that most buyers never notice: the deduction is the only tax benefit you get. Every rupee of interest is taxable. This lesson shows how both work, what they really earn after tax, and the one clever feature of NSC that almost nobody uses.

children.text: National Savings Certificate: How It Works

NSC (VIII Issue) is a 5-year certificate sold by India Post and backed by the Government of India. You invest a lump sum, interest compounds every year, and you get everything back at maturity. The rate is fixed on the day you buy, so a 7.7% NSC bought in September 2026 keeps paying 7.7% for 5 years even if the government cuts rates in October. The minimum is ₹1,000, there is no maximum, and investments up to ₹1,50,000 count under Section 123 (80C). Only resident individuals can buy it.

body.caption: ₹1,000 in NSC at 7.7% grows to ₹1,449 in 5 years.

body.title: Your Turn: NSC Maturity
body.prompt: Gaurav, a pharmacist in Nashik, buys NSC worth ₹50,000 at 7.7%. What will he receive at maturity after 5 years? Round to the nearest rupee.
body.explanation: ₹50,000 × (1.077)^5 = ₹50,000 × 1.44903 = ₹72,452. His interest over 5 years is ₹22,452, all of it taxable at his slab.

children.text: The NSC Feature Almost Nobody Uses

NSC interest is not paid out each year. It is treated as reinvested in the certificate. Because of that, the interest accrued in years 1 to 4 counts as a fresh 80C investment in each of those years, and is also taxable as income in the same year. The two roughly cancel out. The interest for year 5 is paid out at maturity, so it is taxable but not deductible.

body.caption: ₹1,50,000 in NSC at 7.7%: yearly accrued interest and its tax treatment

body.text: If you declare NSC interest every year, the reinvested interest also fills part of your 80C limit in years 1 to 4, reducing the fresh money you need to invest. If you skip it and report all ₹67,355 at maturity instead, you lose the yearly deduction and may be pushed into a higher tax bill in a single year. Declare it yearly under income from other sources and claim the matching 80C amount.

body.title: NSC Tax Check
body.question: Shalini bought ₹1,50,000 of NSC in May 2026. Which statement about her tax treatment is correct?
options: NSC interest is tax-free because NSC is a government scheme
The interest accrued each year for years 1 to 4 is taxable and also eligible for 80C
Only the year 5 interest is eligible for 80C
She can claim ₹2,17,355 under 80C at maturity
body.explanation: Government backing does not make interest tax-free. NSC interest is taxable every year. The interest for years 1 to 4 is deemed reinvested, so it also qualifies under 80C in those years. The final year's interest is paid out, so it is taxable without any matching deduction.

children.text: Tax Saver FDs: Bank and Post Office

A tax saver FD is a 5-year fixed deposit with a scheduled bank that qualifies under Section 123 (80C) up to ₹1,50,000 a year. The Post Office 5-year Time Deposit offers the same deduction. Both look like normal FDs, but the lock-in makes them behave very differently.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: If a tax saver FD is held jointly by a husband and wife, only the ___ holder can claim the Section 123 (80C) deduction.
body.explanation: The deduction goes to the first holder, so put the FD in the name of the spouse who is on the old regime and in the higher slab.

body.text: Post Office TD interest is paid out every year, so the ₹57,851 total assumes you spend it. If you reinvest each payout at a similar rate, the TD's 5-year value comes very close to NSC's. Senior citizens usually get 0.50% extra on bank tax saver FDs, but for them SCSS, covered in the next lesson, is typically the stronger 80C option.

cards.definition: Banks deduct 10% TDS if interest from that bank crosses ₹50,000 in the tax year (₹1,00,000 for senior citizens). Now under Section 393 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (194A under the 1961 Act).
From 1 April 2026, a single Form 121 replaces Forms 15G and 15H for asking the bank not to deduct TDS when your total income is below the taxable limit.
No TDS is deducted on NSC interest, but that does not make it tax-free. You must report and pay tax on it yourself.
Allowed only on the holder's death, by court order, or on forfeiture by a pledgee. Otherwise, you wait 5 years.
NSC can be pledged to a bank as security for a loan. Bank tax saver FDs cannot be used for a loan.
Bank FDs are insured by DICGC up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, including interest. NSC and Post Office TD are backed directly by the government.

body.title: Scenario: The Safe Choice
body.scenario: Rohit, 29, is an accountant in Indore on the old regime, in the 20% slab. After EPF and a term insurance premium, his 80C gap is ₹60,000. He does not want any market risk. He is planning his wedding in about 3 years and may need these savings then. His bank relationship manager suggests a ₹60,000 tax saver FD.
body.prompt: Is the tax saver FD a good fit? What would you advise?
body.modelAnswer: Not if the money may be needed for the wedding in 3 years. Tax saver FDs, NSC and Post Office TDs all lock money for 5 years with no early exit, and a bank tax saver FD cannot even be used for a loan. If the ₹60,000 is truly spare for 5 years, NSC at 7.7% beats the bank FD: about 6.10% after tax at his slab against about 5.27% for ICICI's 6.50% FD, and NSC can be pledged if he is in a pinch. If he can commit longer, PPF at 7.1% tax-free is better still. If the money is wedding money, he should skip the 80C product and keep it in a regular FD or liquid fund. The tax saved, ₹60,000 × 20.8% = ₹12,480, is not worth being unable to access his money when he needs it.

body.title: Before You Buy NSC or a Tax Saver FD
steps: Confirm you are on the old regime and actually have an 80C gap
Be sure you will not need this money for 5 full years
Compare the current NSC and Post Office TD rates with your bank's tax saver FD rate
For a joint FD, make the old-regime, higher-slab spouse the first holder
Submit Form 121 to the bank if your total income is below the taxable limit, so TDS is not deducted
Record the interest accrued each year and report it in your return, even where no TDS is deducted
Save the NSC certificate or FD receipt with your 80C proofs

points: NSC (7.7%), Post Office 5-year TD (7.5%) and bank tax saver FDs (about 6.35% to 6.50% at large private banks) all qualify under Section 123 (80C).
All three lock money for 5 years, and bank tax saver FDs allow no loan or premature withdrawal.
Interest on all three is fully taxable, so after-tax returns at the 30% slab fall to roughly 4.6% to 5.3%.
NSC interest for years 1 to 4 is deemed reinvested, so it is both taxable and eligible under 80C each year.
Only the first holder of a joint tax saver FD can claim the deduction.
For long horizons, PPF's tax-free 7.1% usually beats these options after tax; for money needed within 5 years, skip them.
